chunks: "A mux, short for multiplexer, is a digitally controlled switch.
It has N data inputs, some select lines, and one output, and the select lines decide which input gets passed through to the output.
The simplest one is a 2-to-1 mux: if the select is 0 the output follows input A, if it's 1 the output follows input B.
As an equation that's Y equals not-S times A, plus S times B.
The number of select lines is log base 2 of the number of inputs, so a 4-to-1 mux has two select bits, an 8-to-1 has three, and so on.
You can build bigger muxes out of small ones in a tree, so a 16-to-1 is five 4-to-1 muxes. At gate level a 2-to-1 is an inverter, two ANDs and an OR.
In CMOS you'd normally use two transmission gates, so it's only a handful of transistors.
Where you see them: choosing between register sources, picking which ALU result to use, steering ADC channels with an analog mux, and every if-else in RTL synthesizes to one.
The thing I'd add is that a mux is also a universal logic element.
Feed the data pins with constants and the select lines with your variables, and you've built a look-up table, which is literally what an FPGA is made from.
And a mux can glitch if the select changes while both data inputs are high, because the inverted select arrives late."
